## Learning in Standard GPs

As shown in @sec-kernel-hyperparams, the GP hyperparameters $\vtheta$ are learned by maximising the LML. It is worth seeing explicitly how this LML arises by integrating out the latent function values $\vf$.

Starting from the GP prior $\vf \mid \vX \sim \mathcal{N}(\vzero, K_{\vtheta})$ and likelihood $\vy \mid \vf \sim \mathcal{N}(\vf, \sigma_n^2 \vI)$, Gaussian–Gaussian conjugacy [@bernardo_bayesian_2000] allows the integral over function values to be computed in closed form:
$$
p(\vy \mid \vX, \vtheta) = \int p(\vy \mid \vf) p(\vf \mid \vX, \vtheta) \, d\vf = \mathcal{N}(\vy \mid \vzero, K_{\vtheta} + \sigma_n^2 \vI),
$$ {#eq-gp_marginal_likelihood}

giving the LML of @eq-log-marginal-likelihood. As the product of two Gaussians is proportional to a Gaussian, the $\vf$-integral collapses to a single multivariate normal with covariance $K_{\vtheta} + \sigma_n^2 \vI$.

Hyperparameters can then be found via gradient ascent. The gradient with respect to $\theta_j$ is [@rasmussen_gaussian_2008]:

$$
\frac{\partial \log p(\vy)}{\partial \theta_j} = \frac{1}{2}\tr\left((\valpha \valpha^\top - K_y^{-1}) \frac{\partial K_y}{\partial \theta_j}\right),
$$ {#eq-gradient}

where $\valpha = K_y^{-1} \vy$ and $K_y = K_{\vtheta} + \sigma_n^2 \vI$. The matrix $\valpha \valpha^\top - K_y^{-1}$ has a clear interpretation: $\valpha \valpha^\top$ is a rank-one outer product that captures how the data predicts itself under the current model, while $K_y^{-1}$ reflects the full model uncertainty; a large positive difference for $\partial K_y / \partial \theta_j$ indicates that increasing $\theta_j$ improves the data fit more than it increases model complexity. This follows from the matrix calculus identities $\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \log|K| = \tr(K^{-1} \frac{\partial K}{\partial \theta})$ and $\frac{\partial K^{-1}}{\partial \theta} = -K^{-1} \frac{\partial K}{\partial \theta} K^{-1}$.

Each gradient step requires $K_y^{-1}$, computed via Cholesky decomposition at $O(n^3)$ cost with $O(n^2)$ storage [@rasmussen_gaussian_2008]. For smaller datasets this is typically feasible; however, as datasets grow, $O(n^3)$ scaling becomes prohibitive for large datasets.
